A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Latte research, retaining its core attention formulation and identifiable experiments. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original LRA classification, OpenWebText and Enwik8 language-modeling results, runtime measurements, and latent-size experiments.

after.justification: v3 reports original component comparisons, language-modeling and LRA results, BookCorpus extrapolation experiments, Gemma adaptation, latent-state analyses, and runtime measurements.

M1.justification: The basic Latte formulation is retained, but v3 adds Macchiato's learned mixture of global latent attention and local sliding-window attention, convolutional and RGLRU extensions, RMSNorm/GLU variants, and VAPOR positional rotations. Section 4.5 also introduces adaptation of pretrained Gemma by training Latte-specific parameters.

E1.justification: OpenWebText and the five evaluated LRA tasks remain. v3 removes Enwik8 character-level language modeling and adds BookCorpus, including truncation and unseen-length tests, plus SlimPajama training and evaluation on SlimPajama, Pile, and Tiny-Stories. This substantially changes corpus and test-scenario coverage.

E2.justification: The language-model comparisons expand to Transformer++, Mega, RetNet, H3, RWKV, Griffin, Mamba, and the RGLRU-SWA++ control (v3 Tables 1–2). LRA adds Longformer, BigBird, Linear Transformer, Luna, Mega-Chunk, and S5, while removing Performer and the Best-LRA aggregate from the corresponding comparison (v1 Table 2 versus v3 Table 3).

E3.justification: Reported OpenWebText training changes from 60,000 iterations with batch size 8 to 100,000 with batch size 80, alongside revised model configurations (both versions' Table 5). LRA settings also change; Retrieval's hidden dimension changes from 256 to 128 and learning rate from 0.001 to 0.0001. New protocols include fixed-token-budget comparisons, full-model forward-pass benchmarks, and train-short/test-long evaluation.

E4.justification: v3 adds component comparisons for the ++ modifications, convolution/RGLRU processing, sliding-window attention, and removing Latte (Tables 1–2). It also adds latent-count versus perplexity, truncation, extrapolation, and latent-collapse analyses (Figures 5–7 and 11). The original latent-count versus runtime analysis is retained as Figure 10.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 2 reports runtime means over 100 runs. v3 retains those averaging practices and adds explicit standard-deviation error bars from 100 runs for the new Figure 4 benchmark. Neither version reports training-seed variability or confidence intervals for model-quality results.

E6.justification: v1's OpenWebText comparison reports PPL 27.60 for Latte and 25.53 for attention; v3 reports 21.88 for base Latte, 17.64 for its best hybrid, and 17.19 for Transformer++, under changed architectures and training settings. LRA results are revised, including Retrieval from 50.60 in both old Latte rows to 73.39 in the new base row. Gemma and other new results are added, while Enwik8 results and the original learning curves disappear.

T1.justification: Beyond the retained Latte factorization and recurrences, v3 formally defines Macchiato's L+1-state mixture and local-window distribution, introduces temporally conditioned probabilities, and derives VAPOR's rotation factorization preserving linear complexity (Sections 2.3–2.4 and Appendix B.3). These are substantive mathematical extensions; the original numerical-stability derivation is retained in the appendix.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the contribution from a linear-time attention replacement to a framework combining local and global attention and extending pretrained language models' usable contexts with modest additional training. These are substantial new contribution claims beyond the retained efficiency and comparable-performance claims.

C2.justification: v3 explains how missing elementwise comparisons can weaken local-information modeling and motivates convolutional, recurrent, and local-attention components as remedies. Its LRA discussion also distinguishes improvements on discrete tasks from continuing weaknesses on image tasks relative to state-space models. This substantially extends v1's speed/capacity discussion and unexplained Retrieval failure.

D1.justification: v3 adds sequence-packing instructions, expanded configuration tables, Gemma adaptation resources and training details, and CPU/GPU generation procedures. The original Jax scan listing is retained in Appendix D. Documentation remains imperfect: the repository reference is a placeholder, and Appendix A.1's 50,267-token vocabulary conflicts with Table 5's 57K description.

R1.justification: v3 replaces much of the detailed Linformer/Perceiver/Performer discussion with treatment of Efficient Attention, Luna, and recurrent/hybrid models. It explicitly acknowledges Shen et al.'s equivalent bidirectional formulation and positions its contribution around the latent-variable interpretation, causal extension, local/global integration, and pretrained-model adaptation.

P1.justification: The introduction, method exposition, related work, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before experiments, language modeling replaces LRA as the first experimental topic, and complexity and numerical-stability material move into reorganized appendices covering experimental details, theory, efficiency, and implementation.

P2.justification: The main text switches from two columns to one and gains recurrence and architecture diagrams, runtime bars, extrapolation curves, latent-state heatmaps, and expanded comparison tables. Original runtime plots move into Appendix C, while v1's learning curves are removed. These changes substantially alter the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v1 largely anticipates applicability to larger models and longer unseen contexts; v3 supplies BookCorpus extrapolation tests and pretrained Gemma adaptation evidence. Component controls and contemporary comparators substantially strengthen the empirical case, while acknowledgment of equivalent prior bidirectional attention improves research positioning. These address important gaps in evidence and attribution, outweighing the loss of Enwik8 coverage and remaining configuration inconsistencies and repository-access limitations.
